meta_desc: Understand Class 5 Maths Does It Look the Same? Learn line and rotational symmetry through rangoli and mandala examples, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: NCERT Class 5 Chapter 5 turns the symmetry hiding in rangoli, mandalas and the Ashoka Chakra into something a ten-year-old can fold, turn and name. Here is a plain-language walk-through, two solved case studies, and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 5 child a paper rangoli stencil, ask them to fold it down the middle, and watch what happens: the two halves land exactly on top of each other. That one fold is the whole heart of Class 5 Maths Does It Look the Same? — NCERT’s Chapter 5, which takes the symmetry hiding in kolams, mandalas and the Ashoka Chakra and turns it into something a ten-year-old can fold, turn, name and draw.

What I like about this chapter is that it refuses to start with a definition. It starts with an action. Fold a shape and see if the halves match. Turn a shape and see if it looks unchanged. Hold a mirror against a design and see if the reflection fits. The vocabulary — line of symmetry, reflection, rotation — arrives only after the child has already felt the idea in their hands. Below I unpack the three big ideas, then solve two case studies of exactly the kind the exam uses.

What ‘Does It Look the Same?’ covers

The chapter has two halves that sound similar but are not. The first is line (or mirror) symmetry — can you draw a line that splits a shape into two matching, mirror-image halves? The second is rotational symmetry — if you spin the shape a part-turn about its centre, does it look the same as before you turned it? A shape can have one, both, or neither. That last point trips up more children than any other, so it is worth saying out loud early.

Line symmetry: the fold-and-mirror test

A line of symmetry is a fold line. If you can fold a figure so one half sits perfectly on the other, that fold is a line of symmetry. A square has four such lines; a rectangle has only two; the letter A has one; the letter R has none at all.

More than one mirror line

Rangoli is the perfect teaching tool here because a good rangoli often has several mirror lines meeting at the centre. Ask the child to hunt for all of them, not just the obvious vertical one. A six-petal mandala, for instance, has six lines of symmetry. Counting them is far more useful than memorising that ‘a square has four’.

Reflection is the same idea, standing up

Reflection just means holding a mirror on the line instead of folding. The half you see plus its reflection rebuilds the whole design. In practice, folding is easier for younger children and a small mirror is a lovely check afterwards.

Rotational symmetry: turns of a half, a quarter and a third

This is the fresher, trickier idea. Fix a shape at its centre and rotate it. If it looks identical before a full turn is complete, it has rotational symmetry. The chapter talks in fractions of a turn, and these are worth learning as a set:

  • A half turn is 180° — the letter S and the letter N look the same after a half turn.
  • A quarter turn is 90° — a square looks the same after every quarter turn.
  • A one-third turn is 120° — an equilateral triangle and a three-armed pattern match after a third of a turn.

The Ashoka Chakra on our flag is the classic example: with 24 evenly spaced spokes, it looks the same after a turn of one twenty-fourth. Children find it genuinely surprising that a shape can have rotational symmetry but no mirror line — a paper pinwheel or the recycling arrows are exactly this. Point one out and the idea sticks for good.

Case study 1: Meena’s Diwali rangoli

Here is a worked passage of the sort the case-study workbook is built around. Meena draws a square rangoli. Inside it she paints a design that has 4 lines of symmetry and looks the same after a quarter turn.

Q1. How many lines of symmetry does Meena’s design have? The passage states it plainly: 4. Two run through the mid-points of opposite sides, two along the diagonals.

Q2. Through how many degrees is a quarter turn? A full turn is 360°, so a quarter turn is 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

Q3. If the design looks the same after every quarter turn, how many times does it match in one full turn? Four times — at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. We say its order of rotational symmetry is 4.

Case study 2: The folded paper cut-out

Ravi folds a square sheet in half, then in half again, and snips a small shape from the folded corner. He opens it out.

Q1. How many identical holes appear when he unfolds it? One fold makes 2 layers, a second fold makes 4 layers, so one snip cuts through 4 layers — 4 matching holes.

Q2. Where do the holes sit? Symmetrically around the centre, because each fold created a line of symmetry. The result has both mirror lines and rotational symmetry.

These case studies show the exam pattern: a short real-life passage, then two or three questions that make the child apply the fold-and-turn ideas rather than recite them.

Why Class 5 Maths Does It Look the Same? is worth the extra practice

Symmetry looks like a soft, no-numbers chapter, so families skip it. That is a mistake. It quietly builds the spatial reasoning that geometry, fractions of a turn (angles), and even later coordinate work all lean on. Here is a quick map of the chapter’s ideas against everyday Indian examples.

IdeaQuick testEveryday example
Line symmetryFold — do halves match?A butterfly, the letter M
Several mirror linesCount every fold that worksSix-petal mandala
Half turn (180°)Looks same upside down?The letters S and N
Quarter turn (90°)Looks same after a 90° spin?A square tile
Rotation without mirrorTurns match, folds do notA pinwheel, recycling arrows

One honest caveat from teaching this: do not let a child assume that mirror symmetry and rotational symmetry always come together. They often do — a square has both — but the pinwheel proves they are separate ideas. Testing each one on its own is the habit that earns full marks.

quiz.title: Class 5 Does It Look the Same? Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on line symmetry, mirror lines and rotational turns. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
questions.explanation: A square folds onto itself along both diagonals and both lines through the mid-points of opposite sides — 4 in all.

questions.q: A shape looks the same after a half turn. How many degrees is a half turn?
questions.explanation: A full turn is 360 degrees, so a half turn is 360 divided by 2, which is 180 degrees.

questions.q: Which capital letter has NO line of symmetry?
questions.explanation: A, H and T each fold onto themselves along a mirror line. R does not — no fold makes its halves match.

questions.q: A quarter turn is a rotation of how many degrees?
questions.explanation: A full turn is 360 degrees, so a quarter turn is 360 divided by 4, which is 90 degrees.

questions.q: A six-petal mandala with equal petals has how many lines of symmetry?
questions.explanation: Each petal lines up a fold, so a regular six-petal design has 6 lines of symmetry meeting at the centre.

questions.q: An equilateral triangle looks the same after a turn of one-third. That turn is how many degrees?
questions.explanation: One-third of a full turn is 360 divided by 3, which is 120 degrees.

questions.q: Ravi folds a square sheet in half twice, then makes one snip. How many matching holes appear when he unfolds it?
questions.explanation: One fold gives 2 layers, a second fold gives 4 layers, so a single snip cuts 4 layers and makes 4 holes.

questions.q: Which of these has rotational symmetry but NO line of symmetry?
questions.explanation: A pinwheel looks the same as you turn it, but no fold makes its halves match — rotation without any mirror line.

faq.q: What is Chapter 5 ‘Does It Look the Same?’ about in Class 5 Maths?
faq.a: It teaches two kinds of symmetry: line (mirror) symmetry, where a fold splits a shape into matching halves, and rotational symmetry, where a shape looks unchanged after a part-turn. NCERT uses rangoli, mandalas and everyday designs so the idea stays hands-on.

faq.q: What is the difference between line symmetry and rotational symmetry?
faq.a: Line symmetry is about folding — can you fold the shape so both halves match? Rotational symmetry is about turning — does the shape look the same after you spin it part of a full turn? A shape can have one, both, or neither.

faq.q: How do you find the order of rotational symmetry?
faq.a: Turn the shape through a full circle and count how many times it looks exactly the same, including the starting position. A square matches 4 times, so its order is 4. A pinwheel with three arms matches 3 times.

faq.q: Why does the chapter use rangoli and the Ashoka Chakra?
faq.a: They are familiar Indian designs packed with symmetry, so children can spot mirror lines and turns in something they already know. The Ashoka Chakra, with 24 even spokes, is a memorable example of strong rotational symmetry.
